item.title: Contraposition
item.description:
Recall that the CONTRAPOSITIVE of an implication is as follows, $P \Rightarrow Q \equiv \neg Q \Rightarrow \neg P$. We prove by way of contraposition that if $n^2$ is even, then $n$ is even also.


Proof.   Suppose $n \in \mathbb{Z}$ is odd, that is, $ n = 2k + 1 $ for some $ k \in \mathbb{Z} $. We thus have

$$ n^2 = (2k + 1)^2 = 2(2k^2 + 2k) + 1.$$

Since $n^2$ is of the form $2m + 1,\ m \in \mathbb{Z}$, it follows $n^2$ is odd. Since the contrapositive holds, so does our original claim. Hence if $n^2$ is even, then $n$ is even. $\blacksquare$


Notice that the converse claim need not be proven by contraposition, and can be proven directly with some algebraic manipulation. As an exercise, attempt to prove the claim directly and observe why it is impossible to do so.

Show that if $c > \frac{49}{8}$ then $y = 2x^2 + 7x + c$ has no real roots. Proceed by contraposition.


Proof.   We show that if $y = 2x^2 + 7x + c$ has real roots, then $c \le \frac{49}{8}$. A quadratic polynomial $ ax^2 + bx + c = 0 $ has real roots if and only if $ b^2 - 4ac \ge 0 $. Let $a = 2$ and $b = 7 $. We obtain $7^2 - 4(2c) = 49 - 8c \ge 0$, thus $ c \le \frac{49}{8} $. Since the contrapositive holds, so does our original claim. Hence if $c > \frac{49}{8}$ then $y = 2x^2 + 7x + c$ has no real roots. $\blacksquare$

item.title: Infinitude of the Primes
item.description:
By way of contradiction, we prove that there exists infinitely many primes in $ \mathbb{N} $.


Proof.   Suppose for contradiction that there exists finitely many primes $ p_1, \dots, p_n $. Let $ P = p_1 p_2 \cdots p_n + 1$. Since $ P > 1$, there exists a prime $q$ such that $ q \mid P $. However since dividing $ P $ by any $ p_i $ leaves remainder $1$, it follows that $q$ is a prime not in $p_1, \dots, p_n $, contradicting the assumption that $p_1, \dots, p_n$ contains all primes. Hence the set of primes is infinite. $\blacksquare$


Note that $ p_i \mid p_1 p_2 \cdots p_n $, which implies $ P = p_1 p_2 \cdots p_n + 1$ is one more than a multiple of $ p_i $. Moreover, whether $P$ is prime is irrelevant within the context of our proof.

Our proof need not be by contradiction. Its original formulation by Euclid is direct.

item.title: Monotone Convergence Theorem
item.description:
Let $a:\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}\ \{a_n\}$ be a sequence of real numbers. If $\{a_n\}$ is MONOTONICALLY INCREASING, that is for all $n \in \mathbb{N}, \ a_{n+1} \ge a_n$, and BOUNDED ABOVE, that is for all $n,\ a_n \le B$ for some $B \in \mathbb{R}$, then $\{a_n\}$ converges to a finite value as $n \to \infty$. Likewise if $\{a_n\}$ is MONOTONICALLY DECREASING, that is for all $n \in \mathbb{N}, \ a_{n+1} \le a_n$, and BOUNDED BELOW, that is for all $n, \ a_n \ge b$ for some $b \in \mathbb{R}$, then $\{a_n\}$ converges to a finite value as $n \to \infty$.

We prove each case separately. For both cases, we want to show that, by DEFINITION OF CONVERGENCE,

$$\exists L \in \mathbb{R} \text{ s.t. } \forall \varepsilon > 0, \ \exists N \in \mathbb{N} \text{ s.t. } \forall n \geq N, \ |a_n - L| < \varepsilon.$$

The definition essentially states that a sequence $\{a_n\}$ is convergent if there exists a point $L$ such that beyond some index $N$, every term of the sequence lies within an arbitrary distance $\varepsilon$ of $L$ and never escapes that bound.


Proof.   Since $\{a_n\}$ is nonempty and bounded above, by the LEAST-UPPER-BOUND PROPERTY of $\mathbb{R}$, there exists a least upper bound $L$ of $\{a_n\},\ L = \sup \{a_n\}$. Let $\varepsilon > 0$. Since $L$ is the least upper bound of $\{a_n\},\ L - \varepsilon$ is not an upper bound, hence $\exists N \in \mathbb{N} \text{ s.t. } a_N > L - \varepsilon$.

Since $\{a_n\}$ is monotonically increasing, $\forall n \ge N,\ a_n \ge a_N > L - \varepsilon$. Moreover since $L = \sup\{a_n\}$ is an upper bound of $\{a_n\}, \ \forall n \ge N,\ a_n \leq L < L + \varepsilon$.

Combining the above, $\forall n \ge N, \ L - \varepsilon < a_n < L + \varepsilon\ \implies \forall n \ge N, \ |a_n - L| < \varepsilon$. Since $\varepsilon > 0$ was arbitrary, by definition of convergence, $\{a_n\}$ converges to $L$. $\blacksquare$


The decreasing case is effectively the mirror image of the increasing case—making use of the greatest lower bound in place of the least upper bound—and is left as an exercise for the reader.

Note that in our proof, we make use of the fact that if for all $n \in \mathbb{N},\ a_{n+1} \ge a_n$, then for all $n \ge N,\ a_n \ge a_N$. While trivial, proving it makes for a good exercise. Proceed by induction on $n$.


Proof.   For the base case $n=N$, it immediately follows that $a_n \ge a_N$. For the inductive step, suppose $a_k \ge a_N$ for some $k \ge N$. Since $a_{k+1} \ge a_k$, it follows that $a_{k+1} \ge a_k \ge a_N$, therefore $a_{k+1} \ge a_N$, as needed. Hence for all $n \ge N, \ a_n \ge a_N$. $\blacksquare$

item.title: About
item.description:
I am a second-year Mathematics student at the University of Toronto, St. George. My research interests include:

  • Algebraic Number Theory
  • Category Theory
  • Combinatorics
  • Differential Geometry
  • Ergodic Theory
  • Harmonic Analysis
  • Low-Dimensional Topology
  • Random Matrix Theory
  • Representation Theory

Among other areas.

Prior to beginning my undergrad at the University of Toronto, I competed in the FIRST Robotics Competition, reaching the regional finals with my team. I have also been involved in Model UN, theater and improv performance, and pure mathematics through the UofT Math Academy program.

I am a lifelong learner with broad interests across languages, technology, and the arts. I am a native speaker of English and French, and am currently studying Russian and Mandarin Chinese. In my free time, I am a seasoned skier with 16 years of experience; I also play ultimate frisbee as a member of the UofT Intramurals team, cube, read, play chess, write poetry, and build upon my Linux system.

I am actively seeking undergraduate research opportunities in mathematics. If you are a faculty member working in any of the above areas and are open to working with an undergraduate, I would welcome the chance to connect.
